story_text.value:
Hi HN. I built 1667 for my own fiction work and now use it each day. This probably has a limited audience. Maybe an audience of one...

Why a terminal interface for story writing? I'm a dev. I like to use terminals for a lot of stuff. Most WebUIs feel off to me. That's the only reason.

One thing that bothers me about writing in existing tools is that they don't fit the way I write. The mental model of my story is a tree. I try many takes usually continue with just one, but sometimes I want to try an alternate route and see where this goes. And that can branch again in many places. See what happens if I kill off this character or they don't take the job or whatever.

1667 is a full-screen terminal app for long-form fiction. Each story part can have several takes. All takes stay in a tree. You select one path through that tree as the story line. Export writes that line to Markdown in the project folder.

Some technical details: - A project stores its stories and settings in a `.1667/` directory. Exported Markdown sits beside it. - Provider secrets stay in private machine files. Requests go to the provider that the writer selects. - An optional Vault Password seals project files at rest. - An operating-system lock permits one writer process for each project. - The request viewer shows the next provider request without its credential. - Each generated take keeps a Generation Record with its model and effective settings.

Version 0.9.5 runs on macOS, Linux, and Windows x64. The website has Shell and PowerShell installers. An npm package is also available.

1667 imports Markdown, SillyTavern chats and cards, and NovelAI archives. It can use OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic, and local endpoints such as Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, and KoboldCpp.

Current limits: the release is pre-1.0. The interface is a terminal. There is no account or cloud sync, and I don't plan to add any. No tracking.

title.value: Show HN: 1667, a terminal UI for writing fiction with language models

story_text.value:
Agents needs to store context, and share context. We haven't yet figured out how to do muli-agent swarms in a good way, but letting agents synchronize durably seems to be a key point, a problem which needs a solution regardless. So I decided to separate the concerns and tackle this bit before trying to build a swarm.

Slivingdoc is git + s3 combined into a "hot path". Conflict resolution via git, persistent storage + backup via s3. Agents + humans see gitlike-semantics, without needing to worry about the complexities. See website above for details.

Intended to be run as cli or mcp server (stdio).

story_text.value:
Hey HN! I built https://callmylaptop.com, an app that lets you access the coding agents running on your laptop by phone.

Call My Laptop has three key features: 1) it gives your laptop its own phone number, 2) it lets you start a new or resume an existing Codex, Claude Code, or OpenCode session by phone, and 3) it calls you when a task finishes or needs your input.

I hope Call My Laptop makes coding agents easier and more fun to use away from your desk. I've personally been using it a bunch when I'm riding my bike to spin up sessions on random ideas :).

Happy to chat about the voice, telephony, or dev stack behind the product. Let me know if you have questions, comments, or feature requests!

story_text.value:
I make this tool, a self-hosted dashboard, to show which host ports are taken, as a traffic-light grid. All the reason because I'm a home server enthusiast, but have a chaotic and terrible memory.
It can aggregate ports from your different hosts and VPS as long as the network is reachable. And it merges three local sources into one grid: host listen tables, Docker API, and Compose files.
As a beginner, I am open to everyone's comments, and if there are better similar tools, please tell me about them to help me refer to them for learning, thanks.

I've seen a few of those "Every fucking website in 202*" examples on here the last few days, and I feel it deep in my bones.

As a result of the constant auto-play videos, CTAs, cookie warnings etc. etc., this is probably the most used self-developed app I run. It's super simple - just drop in the URL of the article and it'll extract (maintaining structure, formatting, pullquotes, images etc.) and save into an SQLite library if you want to come back to it later.

Saves nicely as a PWA for tablet / phone reading.
